query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A combined experimental–computational approach—employing high-throughput differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and in-situ X-ray scattering under inert or vacuum conditions, guided by CALPHAD-based simulations—will accurately (within roughly 5–10%) measure the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, the volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for multi-principal-element high-entropy alloys (HEAs) spanning 4–8 components.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-principal-element alloys (≥4 elements) in equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions, with as-cast or homogenized microstructures.
generation.intervention: Systematic high-throughput thermal measurements (DSC) and simultaneous in-situ synchrotron X-ray scattering, both guided and validated by CALPHAD-based predictions, performed across the full composition ranges of candidate HEAs in the ~800–2000 K interval.
generation.conditions: Samples are heated/cooled under controlled inert or vacuum environments with carefully calibrated DSC protocols and complementary synchrotron X-ray diffraction to track phase evolution near and through melting.
generation.structural_mediator: Direct diffraction tracking of phase boundaries and lattice parameters in real time mediates between the thermal signals from DSC and the simulated phase equilibria from CALPHAD calculations.
generation.mechanism: By synchronizing enthalpy and entropy data from DSC with real-time phase characterization and CALPHAD-based Gibbs energy evaluations, the approach captures both thermodynamic (enthalpy, entropy) and volumetric (from X-ray scattering) responses at the melting transition, yielding robust liquid-phase property data.
generation.predicted_outcome: Tm, ΔHfus, ΔSfus, and ΔVfus determined to within ~5–10% of their true values for a wide variety of HEAs; the approach will expedite rapid mapping of composition–property correlations for liquid-phase thermodynamics and melting behavior.
generation.baseline: Conventional single-alloy DSC or separate modeling approaches often require extensive trial and error for each alloy. Coupling a high-throughput screening platform with validated CALPHAD modeling offers greater speed and consistency in measuring and predicting thermophysical properties across broad composition spaces.
generation.boundary: Applicable primarily to extensively calibrated thermodynamic databases and alloys whose phases form near-equilibrium during DSC experiments. Metastable or rapidly heated systems could deviate if transient phases obscure DSC or X-ray measurements.
generation.uncertainty: Exact error margins depend on the precision of DSC calibration, sample homogeneity, the accuracy of the thermodynamic database, and potential unaccounted transient phase transformations.

falsification_experiment.design: Independently measure the same set of HEA compositions using a different technique, for instance, precision drop calorimetry with ex-situ structural characterization (TEM/SEM). Compare the derived thermodynamic parameters and melting points with the integrated DSC–X-ray–CALPHAD predictions.
measurements: Measured Tm, ΔHfus, ΔSfus, and ΔVfus from high-throughput DSC + in-situ X-ray scattering with CALPHAD guidance
Same property measurements from independent drop-calorimetry or neutron diffractometry on matched samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If measured absolute differences in Tm, ΔHfus, or ΔSfus systematically exceed 10% of the reference methods’ average values, then the hypothesis that the integrated approach is reliably accurate within those bounds is rejected.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted a lot of attention in recent years, due to the unique combinations of structural, physical and chemical properties of these alloys [1] – [3] . HEAs usually form simple structures such as body-centered cubic (BCC) (e.g. TaNbHfZrTi [4] , NbTaVWZr [5] etc.) or face-centered cubic (FCC) (e.g., CoCrCuFeNi [6] , CoCrFeMnNi [7] etc.) solid solutions. The large number of the alloying elements in near-equiatomic proportions result in high configurational entropy in these solid solutions. However, these alloys can decompose to multiple phases upon changing the composition or annealing at different temperatures or a combination of both [8] – [10] . Such a phase decomposition is often the result of the complex interplay of configurational entropy of mixing with the enthalpies of mixing of the constituent elements. Additionally, such multiphase microstructures are more likely to exhibit the desired properties for real engineering applications. Hence, tuning the composition and fractions of phases is critical for achieving the desired properties [10] , [11] .

The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. chosen.why: An integrated experimental-computational approach allows accurate direct measurement of thermodynamic properties while leveraging computational models to efficiently explore large composition spaces. This is a standard, well-established strategy in materials science for obtaining Tm, enthalpy, entropy of fusion, volume changes at melting, and complex liquid-phase thermodynamics in high-entropy alloys. It is both comprehensive and validated by consistent cross-checking between experiments and simulations, with any inconsistency serving as a clear indicator to revisit model parametrization or measurement protocols.
